notes:
I've got notes for most verses of Exodus 3. I ran out of research steps before I could read the NET Bible notes page or any Methodist, Lutheran or Pentecostal-denomination sites. I found nothing for vv. 9, 16–17 or 20, so those verses are left out, and the notes on vv. 10, 15, 19 and 21 are thin.

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Moses spent 40 years as an unknown shepherd, and he didn't even own the sheep. Horeb is the mountain later called Sinai; the name probably means "desert" or "desolation." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/
- Ellicott says "father-in-law" really means "relation by marriage." He thinks Jethro was probably Reuel's son, which would make him Moses's brother-in-law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/3.htm
- Modern scholarship: the Cambridge note on Bible Hub assigns parts of the passage to different sources ("P," "J," "E") and says we must not try to fit the J and E stories into P's timeline. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/3-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Who was the Angel? Precept Austin says he is not a created angel but God Himself, and most writers think this is a Christophany (an appearance of Christ before his birth). https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-3-commentary
- Gill argues the same way: the Angel is called Jehovah and calls himself the God of Abraham, which a created angel would never do. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/3-2.htm
- Ellicott: because the angel is called both "Jehovah" and "Elohim" in v. 4, it was, with reason, the Second Person of the Trinity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/3.htm
- Not everyone agrees. Matthew Henry gives both views: some think a created angel speaking for the one who sent him, others the second person, who is himself Jehovah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/3-3.html
- What the bush means:
  - Keil & Delitzsch: it stands for Israel in the "iron furnace" of Egypt, not consumed because Jehovah was in the flame, chastening His people but not giving them over to death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/3-3.htm
  - Guzik adds a second meaning, the cross: Jesus, crowned with thorns, endured the fires of judgment without being consumed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/
- NET Bible note (quoted by Precept Austin): Philo was the first to read the bush as Israel, and the Bible leaves the interpretation open. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-3-commentary
- Reformed history: Ligonier describes the Huguenots putting the burning bush on their church seal with the motto "I burn, but am not consumed." They may also have been taking a jab at the excessive devotion to Mary found among Catholics. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/symbol-burning-bush-church-history
- Orthodox reading: the bush signifies the Mother of God's sinless conception of Christ, and a hymn says that as the bush wasn't consumed, the Virgin gave birth and stayed a virgin. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2014/09/04/102500-unburnt-bush-icon-of-the-mother-of-god
- Catholic reading: an antiphon for the Feast of the Circumcision sees in "the bush that was not burnt" a figure of Mary conceiving her Son without losing her virginity. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/15464b.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott sees the words "turn aside" as a small detail showing Moses wrote the account: he remembered the bush was off his path. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/3.htm
- Precept Austin says natural explanations, such as bright berries or leaves, are not an honest reading of the literal text. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-3-commentary

**v. 4**
- Guzik: God didn't speak until He had Moses' attention. Calling his name twice shows urgency, as with "Abraham, Abraham" and "Samuel, Samuel." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/
- In Hebrew the verse says "when Jehovah saw, Elohim called." Ellicott argues this disproves the theory of two separate writers, because one sentence can't be split between two authors. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/3.htm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: taking off sandals showed humility (servants went barefoot) and recognised God's immediate presence. Because God is holy, there will always be a distance between God and man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/
- Ellicott: people in the ancient East removed sandals in temples and palaces. God Himself orders this respect for the place His presence has made holy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/3.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: "the God of Abraham" implies that the patriarchs still live after death, since He can only be God of things that exist (see Matthew 22:32). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/3.htm
- Guzik: Moses hid his face as one who knew he was not only a creature but a sinful creature. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/

**vv. 7–8**
- Ellicott: "come down" is language that stoops to our limits. Even Jews didn't take it literally (1 Kings 8:27). "Milk and honey" was probably already a common saying for a rich land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/3.htm
- Guzik: God is separate from us, but not distant; He cares and connects Himself to our needs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/

**v. 10**
- Guzik: God says He will rescue Israel, yet He sends Moses. This shows that God often chooses to work through human instruments. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: the people best suited to great missions often think themselves unfit. He compares Jeremiah, Ambrose and Anselm. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/3.htm
- Guzik: God never answers "Who am I?" because the real question is "Who is God?" https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: God answers what Moses meant rather than what he said. In effect: "Not unfit, since I will be with thee." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/3.htm
- What is the "sign"?
  - Guzik thinks it probably points back to the burning bush itself, because the arrival at Sinai came many months later. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/
  - Constable agrees: the sign was evidently the burning bush, and the promise of coming back to the mountain called for faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/3-3.html

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: in polytheistic Egypt every god had a name. Moses feared the Israelites had become Egyptian enough to want one. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/3.htm

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: perhaps this isn't so much a name as a deep and mysterious statement of His nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/3.htm
- Gill: the words cover God's self-existence, eternity, unchangeableness, and faithfulness in keeping His promises. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/3-14.htm
- Piper (Desiring God, Baptist): "Yahweh" and "I AM" come from the same Hebrew word and are used interchangeably here. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/i-am-who-i-am
- Where teachers differ on emphasis:
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel) adds that God is "the becoming one," who becomes whatever we lack in our need. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/
  - The Gospel Coalition (Reformed) describes a different "redemptive-historical" view. On that view God gives the name to tell Israel He will be present to deliver them. It adds that the name may serve that purpose more than defining His being. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/what-yhwy-mean/
- New Testament link: Jesus applies "I AM" to Himself (John 8:58; 18:5–6). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/
- Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey): many scholars connect YHWH with the verb "to be." The text may mean God is self-existent, and the verb form may also suggest a continuing future presence. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/yahweh/

**v. 15**
- Guzik: "forever" stresses God's faithfulness to His covenant. Yahweh appears more than 160 times in Genesis, so it wasn't a new name. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/
- Precept Austin: the name existed before Moses, but its meaning wasn't revealed until his time. This is how it squares v. 15 with Exodus 6:3. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jehovah_-_i_am

**v. 18 (the "three-day journey")**
- Ellicott: they needed to go that far away because the Egyptians held some animals sacred. Killing white cows, for example, was a grave crime in Egypt. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/exodus-3.html
- Was the request deceptive? Constable, quoting another writer, says there was no deceit in it, because Pharaoh knew it meant Israel would not come back. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/3-22.html

**v. 19**
- Guzik: God warns in advance that Pharaoh will refuse, which shows His judgments are purposeful, not haphazard. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-3/

**vv. 21–22 (the "plunder")**
- "Borrow" or "ask"? The Pulpit Commentary says the Hebrew word just means "ask," not "borrow." Another note on the same page points out the jewels were only requested at the very moment Israel was being driven out (Exodus 12:33–36). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/3-22.htm
- Several older commentators, including Gill and Chuck Smith, see the goods as back pay owed for years of slavery. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/3-22.html
- Calvin: God gave nothing that wasn't already His own. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/3-22.html
- The Geneva Study Bible adds a caution: this example may not be followed generally. It was only right because God commanded it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/3-22.htm
- NET Bible: God intended Israel to plunder Egypt as they might a defeated enemy. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?amp=&book=Exo&chapter=3
- Popular modern teaching: I found no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace material on these verses. The closest is a Bible Hub study page that links the verse to Proverbs 13:22 ("the wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous"). It doesn't call this prosperity teaching. https://biblehub.com/study/exodus/3-22.htm
